prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, bringing frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks combine a clear, original idea (magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms so that the light shift cancels) with an experimental programme that took atomic frequency standards to roughly 10^-18, an accuracy that has opened tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and the prospective redefinition of the second. The credit is compact: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength scheme and made the early strontium demonstrations, and Ye's group drove the accuracy and stability frontier and the many-body clock physics. Several laboratories reproduce the performance independently, so the result is mature. As an atomic theorist I can judge directly that the underlying physics, precise atomic structure, polarisabilities and systematic shifts, is solid and demanding rather than incremental. Among the eight shortlisted entries this is the one where the discovery, the attribution and the maturity all line up with the fewest open questions.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is lineage. The 2005 prize (frequency combs) and the 2012 prize (control of single trapped ions) already honour the neighbouring advances, so the committee may read lattice clocks as a continuation rather than a new discovery. Optical-clock leadership is also shared with single-ion clocks and other lattice groups (Lemonde, Lisdat, the Yb groups) that the credited names do not cover, and the SI redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so a purist could argue that the measurement's decisive consequence is still pending. Finally, my first-place ranking comes from my own subfield, and I should be wary of overweighting it.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as an original, field-defining architecture that underlies nearly all superconducting processors, and notes that it follows naturally from the 2025 circuit prize while admitting his own proximity to the area.
responses.response: I agree that circuit QED is a serious, mature candidate and I ranked it third and keep it as my first alternative. I read the closeness to the 2025 prize differently from you: that prize honoured macroscopic quantum tunnelling, which is a distinct discovery, so I do not treat overlap as disqualifying. My hesitation is attribution. The founding 2004 papers include Girvin and Huang, and the Yale transmon and readout work is intertwined with the architecture, so a three-name split leaves real credit unresolved. The clock case is cleaner on that point, and I would give your declared connection to the field some weight when comparing the two.

responses.point: Danielsson regards the clock work as a transformational instrument but weighs it fifth, noting that Hall and Hansch were honoured in 2005 for comb technology and that the pending redefinition of the second could make the timing either ripe or premature.
responses.response: The comb overlap is the point I take most seriously. My view is that the comb is the enabling tool and the lattice clock is a separate physical idea: it solves the problem of trapping many atoms without perturbing the clock transition, which no comb advance did. The 2012 ion-control prize likewise concerned single quantum systems, not a many-atom magic-wavelength scheme. I would not wait for the redefinition, since the discovery already stands on the 10^-18 comparisons between independent laboratories. I also note that you put circuit QED eighth, which I find too low for a work this consequential, though for reasons I do not share if it rests only on the 2025 prize.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first, with Katori proposing the magic-wavelength scheme and Ye bringing it to the accuracy frontier, and flags overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes and the allocation relative to other lattice-clock contributors.
responses.response: We agree on the core and on the two-name configuration. I would add one qualification to your attribution: the early strontium demonstrations came from several groups at about the same time, and the many-body clock work in Ye's lab is a distinct step that I would put in the citation. If the committee wanted to widen the credit, the third seat would be the hardest call and I would not fill it without clear evidence of priority. I would not use that difficulty as a reason to drop the candidate.

responses.point: Pearce puts IceCube first as a new observational window whose decisive difficulty (calibration and background rejection) was solved, and ranks circuit QED second and optical lattice clocks fifth.
responses.response: I respect the instrumental achievement, but I hold reservations about the maturity of the physics case. The diffuse flux is established, yet the origin of most of the flux is unresolved and the source evidence rests on few objects, which you note yourself. Clocks have reached agreement at 10^-18 across laboratories. I also see the IceCube credit as more diffuse than for the clocks, because any three names understate a very large collaboration. I would keep IceCube open as a strong candidate for later, but I would not put it ahead of a result whose attribution and verification are this clean.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.
Whether lattice-clock pioneers outside the credited names (for example Lemonde, Lisdat, Gill) should share credit; I cannot settle priority from the supplied list.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should be awaited or is irrelevant to the discovery.
My ranking of circuit QED against clocks depends on how much weight colleagues give to the 2025 prize and to the unresolved Girvin and Huang credit.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for the preferred configuration: my profile documents no collaboration with Katori or Ye. I do collaborate with Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich, and Andreas Wallraff (credited under circuit QED, my first alternative) is at the same institution, so I flag that institutional proximity as a possible recusal question if B016 advances. My profile documents no direct tie to him.
